assets_or_entry_points.exposure: Any peer that can place Ethernet frames on the segment. This asset is the first boundary at which off-target traffic is discarded, so what it discards and what it does not is stated exactly. CONTROLS PRESENT, each read from the pinned source: (1) the EMAC hardware filters on the destination MAC address, configured for every channel with EMAC_MAC_ADDRESS_MATCH (src/app/driver/emac/emac.c:238), so a frame not addressed to the ECU's MAC is dropped before it reaches the CPU; (2) a frame-type filter is applied before a frame is transferred (NetworkInterface.c:285), and it is active rather than compiled out, because the project sets ipconfigETHERNET_DRIVER_FILTERS_FRAME_TYPES to 1 (src/os/freertos/freertos-plus/freertos-plus-tcp/source/include/FreeRTOSIPConfig.h:275), which selects the real eConsiderFrameForProcessing path at NetworkInterface.c:73 rather than the unconditional eProcessBuffer alternative at NetworkInterface.c:71; (3) the received length is bounded against ipTOTAL_ETHERNET_FRAME_SIZE before the frame is copied (NetworkInterface.c:237) and the destination buffer is allocated to that received length (NetworkInterface.c:226). CONTROLS ABSENT, recorded as observations and deliberately not inflated into a threat: (1) there is no minimum-length check on the receive path at the driver layer. The 60-byte minimum NIC_ETH_MIN_FRAME_BYTES (NetworkInterface.c:79) is applied only in NIC_FormatBuffer on the transmit path (NetworkInterface.c:163-165) and is never applied to an incoming frame, so a short received frame is not rejected here; (2) there is no ingress rate limit, no per-source frame accounting, and no broadcast or multicast policy control anywhere in this driver; (3) the receive path processes only single-buffer-descriptor frames and does not chain descriptors for a fragmented frame, which the code states in a comment and leaves as a TODO (NetworkInterface.c:289-295), so its effect is to bound which frames are processed rather than to validate them. IMPORTANT BOUND ON CONTROL 1, which is the reason this asset does not reduce any threat: a destination-MAC match filter is NOT an access control against an attacker who is already present on the segment. Such an attacker chooses the destination MAC and therefore passes the filter; the filter only excludes traffic originating off-segment. It must not be read as authentication, and there is no credential check, no integrity check, no replay protection and no rate limit anywhere on this path. The MAC filter therefore does not weaken the attacker precondition of THR-001 or THR-002, both of which already require a peer present on the segment. For that reason no new threat ID was derived from this asset, and that decision is recorded in method.limitations rather than left implicit.

assumptions: The analysis assumes the code read at commit 308028fb is the code that is built and deployed. If a downstream integration adds a protocol on the serial receive queue, or a write-capable service on the network interface, the corresponding threats (THR-006, THR-007) must be re-analysed before those ratings may be reused.

The analysis assumes the configured values are the effective values: ETH_ECHO_SERVER_PORT_NUMBER = 7, ETH_ECHO_SERVER_BACKLOG = 1, ETH_ECHO_SERVER_RECEIVE_TIMEOUT = portMAX_DELAY (src/app/application/config/ethernet_cfg.h:90, :85, :94), ipconfigTCP_MSS = 536 (src/os/freertos/freertos-plus/freertos-plus-tcp/source/include/FreeRTOSIPConfig.h:294), and ETH_DEFAULT_DEBUG_MESSAGE_SIZE = 30 (src/app/application/ethernet/ethernet.c:80, which is defined in the module itself rather than in a configuration header). The 30 is the length of the fixed greeting banner and the 536 is the length of the receive buffer; they are separate constants at separate locations and neither is derived from the other. No build was performed and no binary was inspected.

The analysis assumes ipconfigHAS_DEBUG_PRINTF is not enabled. It is not defined in the project's FreeRTOSIPConfig.h, so it takes the default ipconfigDISABLE, which reduces FreeRTOS_debug_printf to a no-op. Under that configuration the latent unterminated-buffer read at ethernet.c:189 is compiled out. If a variant enabled debug printf, that statement would no longer hold and the defect would become live. This is recorded as a configuration-dependent latent defect, NOT as a vulnerability, and no out-of-bounds read is claimed to be reachable in the evidenced configuration.

The analysis assumes the diagnosis engine reports entries as configured. DIAG_ID_CAN_RX_QUEUE_FULL is configured DIAG_EVALUATION_ENABLED with DIAG_SEN_EVENT_1; whether the reporting path is itself functional at runtime was not tested.
The analysis assumes the CAN identifiers in tools/dbc/foxbms.dbc correspond to the receive table compiled into the target. That correspondence was not re-derived for this record.

Reachability of the Ethernet segment, the CAN bus and the serial line is assumed to be a deployment property outside the repository. No rating in this record depends on a specific reachability assumption, and none is asserted.

item_and_scope.item_under_analysis: foxBMS 2 BMS master communication stack: the CAN interface, the FreeRTOS-Plus-TCP Ethernet/TCP application layer (EMAC + PHY + FreeRTOS_Sockets), and the SCI/UART serial interface, together with the host-side engineering toolchain that can write to the target.
item_and_scope.profile_relationship: This TARA is a synthetic_reference artifact. It describes a HYPOTHETICAL project built on the foxBMS 2 baseline. Its threat set is grounded in the real, pinned foxBMS source; its mitigations, requirements and acceptance are forward-engineered judgements of that hypothetical project and do not describe, certify or evaluate the real foxBMS product. The as_is profile deliberately contains no TARA: the real foxBMS 2 project at commit 308028fb contains no threat analysis and no cybersecurity work product, and this record does not change that. No statement here should be read as a claim that the real foxBMS product is secure or insecure in absolute terms; it is a bounded statement about what the pinned source does and does not implement.
item_and_scope.scope_basis: The scope was drawn by enumerating every externally reachable entry point in the pinned source at commit 308028fb and reading the code path from the wire to the first application-visible decision. Each included interface was located with the graft code-search tool and then read directly; every claim below cites file:line evidence recorded in docs/artifacts/sources/source-registry.json as FB2-SRC-COD-000057..000087. Interfaces that exist in the source but were not traced to an application data path are stated as such rather than assumed to be absent.

limitations: This is NOT an ISO/SAE 21434 TARA. No damage scenario per asset, no attack path analysis, no attack tree, no TARA review, and no residual-risk evaluation record exist. The ISO/SAE 21434 reference in standards_mappings names intent only.
No ISO/SAE 21434, ISO 26262, ASPICE or other certification or compliance is claimed, implied or supported by this record.

No penetration test, no fuzzing, no exploit development and no attack was performed. Every threat is a static reading of code. No statement here asserts that any threat is exploitable in a deployed system.

No vulnerability database was consulted and no CVE, CVSS score, exploit or affected-version claim is made for any third-party component. See docs/artifacts/sources/sbom.json for what the component inventory can and cannot support.

Only the dispatch layers of the CAN and UART receive paths were traced. The per-message receive callbacks registered against can_rxMessages[] were NOT individually audited, so this record cannot state whether any individual callback adds its own counter, CRC or plausibility check. Absence of such a check is asserted at the dispatch layer only.

The FreeRTOS-Plus-TCP TCP input processing (src/os/freertos/freertos-plus/freertos-plus-tcp/source/FreeRTOS_TCP_Recv.c) was not line-by-line audited. The consequences claimed for THR-004 are therefore bounded to what the application hook itself shows.

Reachability of the Ethernet segment, the CAN bus and the RS485 wires is a deployment property. The source shows a link-local 169.254.107.24/16 address with no DHCP; this record cannot determine whether any given deployment is reachable from outside the ECU.

The FreeRTOS and FreeRTOS-Plus-TCP trees are vendored and locally modified for the TI TMS570LC43x port. Any statement about the behaviour of those components is a statement about the vendored copy in this repository, not about an upstream release.

The EMAC MAC/PHY ingress path (AST-009) was read to the point of frame delivery to the IP task, and the controls present and absent on it are enumerated in that asset. NO NEW THREAT ID WAS DERIVED FROM IT, and the reason is recorded here rather than left implicit. The only security-relevant property the path adds is that it discards some off-target traffic: a destination-MAC match filter (emac.c:238), a frame-type filter that is active in this configuration (FreeRTOSIPConfig.h:275 selecting NetworkInterface.c:73), and a bound on the received length (NetworkInterface.c:237). None of these is authentication, integrity, replay protection or rate limiting, and the destination-MAC filter is trivially satisfied by any attacker already on the segment because the destination address is chosen by the sender. The attacker precondition of every threat this asset could support is therefore identical to the precondition already stated in THR-001 and THR-002, namely presence on the segment, so a separate threat ID would double-count one exposure and inflate the apparent breadth of this record. The absent controls on this path are recorded as observations in AST-009.exposure. The vendored IP stack's own receive-path processing, including its own minimum-length test in prvProcessEthernetPacket, was NOT audited; the observations in AST-009 are asserted about the driver layer only, and the presence of any further check inside the vendored stack is unknown to this record.
method.method_description: Five steps, all performed by reading the pinned source: (1) enumerate externally reachable entry points by locating every socket, interrupt-driven receive and task-body entry in the master communication stack; (2) for each entry point, read the code from the wire to the first application-visible decision and record, literally, which security control is present and which is absent, with file:line; (3) derive a threat only where the code exhibits a reachable, unmitigated condition, and mark every other threat explicitly as a hypothetical-project judgement not observed in the source; (4) map each threat to preventive / detective / reactive mitigations, recording status 'absent_in_source' wherever the mechanism does not exist; (5) tabulate residual risk per threat and hand the mitigations to the derived security requirements. Where a control could not be established from the source, the record says so rather than assuming either presence or absence.
method.method_name: Corpus-local asset-driven threat enumeration and risk tabulation (source-evidence-first)

mitigations.description: Authenticated and confidential transport for every externally reachable network service of the master. Any peer must prove an identity before a session is serviced, and session data must not be readable on the wire.
mitigations.mechanism: Transport-layer authentication with forward secrecy over a maintained TLS profile, or an application-layer mutually-authenticated session established before any request is served. The mechanism must be applied ahead of the accept-to-task hand-off so that an unauthenticated peer never causes a task to be created.

mitigations.description: Bounded connection admission and resource budget for network services: an allowlist or credential check per peer, a hard cap on concurrently serviced connections, a finite receive timeout, and deterministic release of a connection that exceeds its budget.
mitigations.mechanism: Enforce the cap and the timeout at the point where a connected socket is admitted, and treat a refused admission as a diagnosable event rather than as a silent discard. The finite receive timeout is the specific control that removes the hold-open condition in THR-003; the pinned configuration uses portMAX_DELAY.

mitigations.description: Bounded receive into a fixed-size buffer. Recorded because it is a control that IS present, and a threat analysis that listed only absent controls would misrepresent the code.
mitigations.mechanism: The echo path declares uint8_t rxBuffer[ipconfigTCP_MSS] on the task stack and passes ipconfigTCP_MSS as the receive length on every FreeRTOS_recv call, including the drain call in the shutdown path, so no read can exceed the array. The subsequent send loop is bounded by receivedBytes, which the receive call has already capped.

mitigations.description: Message-level integrity and freshness on safety-relevant bus traffic: a rolling counter, a payload integrity check, and a DLC check applied to every safety-relevant received frame before the receive callback is invoked.
mitigations.mechanism: Applied in the CAN dispatch layer ahead of the callback invocation, so that a frame failing counter continuity, integrity or expected length is rejected and recorded before it can influence any consumer. Rejecting on stale or replayed frames is what makes the counter necessary; the integrity check is what makes the counter non-forgeable by a bus peer.

mitigations.description: Framing, integrity and authorisation on the serial link, and demotion of the XOFF/XON bytes from commands to ordinary data.
mitigations.mechanism: A frame structure with an explicit length field validated before the payload is acted on, an integrity field that a line peer cannot produce without the key, and a receive path in which 0x11 and 0x13 are treated as payload rather than as flow-control commands unless they arrive inside a frame that has already been authenticated. The third clause is the specific control that removes the single-byte transmit-suppression condition in THR-006.

mitigations.description: Cryptographically strong entropy for the network stack's security-relevant parameters, seeded per boot from a non-degenerate source rather than from a compile-time constant.
mitigations.mechanism: A vetted hardware random-number source on the MCU, or a seeding procedure that draws from a source not fixed at build time, feeding the initial sequence number and the stack's random-value hook. The specific defect being corrected is a single 32-bit state seeded with a build-time literal and advanced by a fixed multiplier plus a tick count.

mitigations.description: Diagnosis of CAN receive queue overflow. Recorded because it is a detective control that IS present, enabled and severity-rated, and because it demonstrates that the pattern the UART path lacks is already established elsewhere in the same codebase.
mitigations.mechanism: CAN_RxInterrupt reports DIAG_ID_CAN_RX_QUEUE_FULL with DIAG_EVENT_OK or DIAG_EVENT_NOT_OK depending on whether the enqueue succeeded. The entry is configured in the diagnosis table as DIAG_SEN_EVENT_1, DIAG_WARNING, DIAG_DELAY_DISCARD, DIAG_EVALUATION_ENABLED, so a single dropped frame raises a warning.

mitigations.description: Diagnosable and recoverable handling of communication resource exhaustion: every receive queue and connection-admission failure must raise a diagnosis entry, and a connection that exceeds its budget must be closed deterministically.
mitigations.mechanism: Extend the DIAG_ID_CAN_RX_QUEUE_FULL pattern to the serial receive queue, to the connection-admission path and to the connection-lifetime budget, and act on the entry rather than only reporting it. Detection without a defined response is not a mitigation, which is why this is typed reactive rather than detective.

mitigations.description: Third-party component inventory with a defined owner, and a vulnerability-monitoring process for the components in that inventory.
mitigations.mechanism: A maintained inventory of every third-party component in the target and in the toolchain, each entry carrying the evidence for its version, plus a scheduled process that checks the inventory against an authoritative advisory source and records the result. The inventory itself now exists in this corpus as docs/artifacts/sources/sbom.json; the monitoring process does not. The SBOM deliberately records no vulnerability status, because no advisory source was consulted and inventing one would be a fabrication.

out_of_scope: The analog front end, the cell measurement chain, the SBC, the interlock circuit and the contactor drivers. Out of scope because they are not communication entry points; they appear in this record only as the assets whose assurance a communication injection could undermine.
The BMS slave boards and the isoSPI/SPI daisy chain to the AFEs. Not analysed; this record makes no statement about them.

FreeRTOS kernel and FreeRTOS-Plus-TCP internal correctness. Only the application hooks and the receive length bounds were read. The FreeRTOS_TCP_Recv.c input path was not audited, and no claim is made about the correctness of the vendored stacks.
Physical-layer attacks: bus tapping, glitch injection, fault injection, side-channel analysis and voltage manipulation. Not analysed and not assessed.
The bootloader and the secure-boot chain. Not analysed. THR-008 touches the general supply-chain concern but makes no claim about the bootloader's integrity controls, which were not read.
The host-side Python CLI, its CAN/UART libraries and its database handling. The toolchain appears in this record only as AST-006 and THR-008; the CLI itself was not reviewed.
Availability of the physical product, the host operating system, the browser surface of the tooling, and any service deployed alongside the ECU. Not analysed.

threats.attack_vector: Adjacent host on the same Ethernet link, or any host with a routed path to 169.254.107.24, opens TCP to port 7. The handshake succeeds unconditionally.
threats.description: Unauthenticated, unencrypted TCP session establishment on the echo server. ETH_ListenForConnection calls FreeRTOS_socket/freeRTOS_bind/FreeRTOS_listen and then loops on FreeRTOS_accept (src/app/application/ethernet/ethernet.c:255, :276-283, :286-293). Between accept and the hand-off of the connected socket there is no check of the peer address (clientAddress is filled by accept as an output parameter and never inspected; pParameters is explicitly discarded at :248), no credential exchange, no cryptographic handshake, and no connection-rate limit. No TLS library is present anywhere in the master communication stack. The MAC/PHY ingress path in front of this service (AST-009) was also read: it filters on the destination MAC address (src/app/driver/emac/emac.c:238) and applies a frame-type filter before handing a frame up (NetworkInterface.c:285, active in this configuration per src/os/freertos/freertos-plus/freertos-plus-tcp/source/include/FreeRTOSIPConfig.h:275), but neither is a security control against a peer on the segment, because the destination MAC is chosen by the sender and the frame-type filter discards protocol types rather than authenticating a peer. This threat therefore holds at the MAC layer as well as at the TCP application layer.
honest_unknowns: Whether any deployment puts a routable interface in front of this segment is unknown.
No attempt was made to connect to port 7 on hardware; reachability is inferred from the code and the configured address only.
Whether FreeRTOS-Plus-TCP applies any connection-level rate limit of its own was not audited.

The EMAC does filter on the destination MAC address and does apply a frame-type filter before a frame is handed up (AST-009), but neither was tested on hardware and the frame-type filter is a vendored-stack mechanism whose coverage of this configuration was read from the configuration macro rather than exercised. Neither is an authentication control, and the destination-MAC filter is satisfied by any sender on the segment, so neither reduces the attacker precondition stated in attack_vector.
threats.impact: The peer obtains an established TCP session to the master and an on-target task that services it. The capability granted is limited to the echo service: the received bytes are echoed and are never written to the internal database, so this does NOT by itself permit actuation or measurement manipulation. The concrete impact is occupancy of the single echo-server queue slot and of an echo-server task (see THR-003), and the ability to use the ECU as a fixed-target TCP reflector (see THR-002).
threats.likelihood_impact_reasoning: Impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability of battery data is low, because the evidenced service is a pure echo and the code path from accepted socket to database does not exist. Impact on availability is medium, because the connection occupies a resource that has no admission control (THR-003). Likelihood is deployment-dependent and cannot be rated from source: the interface uses a link-local address with no DHCP and no routed path in the default configuration, so an external attacker requires either physical/logical presence on the link or a deployment that routes the subnet. The corpus cannot resolve this and does not assume either way.
threats.residual_risk_justification: With MIT-001 and MIT-002 implemented in the hypothetical project, an unauthenticated peer is rejected before a task is created, so residual likelihood is governed by the strength of the credential store and by network segmentation, neither of which is defined in this corpus. The rating is therefore bounded to 'the exposure is removed but the compensating segmentation controls are unspecified', and is explicitly not a statement that the residual risk is acceptable.

threats.attack_vector: A third party that can direct traffic at the ECU's IP and port 7 receives that traffic back, giving the ECU a stable, non-rewriting reflector endpoint and a liveness oracle for the segment.
threats.description: The echo server is a byte-reflecting service with a fixed, well-known port and a fixed link-local address. ETH_EchoServerInstance receives N bytes into rxBuffer (src/app/application/ethernet/ethernet.c:175) and returns those same N bytes to the peer (:184-193) with no parsing, no filtering and no content check.
honest_unknowns: No traffic measurement was performed; the absence of amplification is an argument from reading the send loop, not from measurement.
threats.impact: The ECU can be used as a fixed-target reflector. IMPORTANT BOUND: the evidenced echo is one-for-one in the send direction (receivedBytes in, receivedBytes out), so this is NOT a volumetric amplification primitive as the code is written. The reflection property is real; an amplification factor is not evidenced and is not claimed. Separately, the fixed 30-byte banner sent at :151-152 and the verbatim echo make the service trivially fingerprintable. The banner length is the compile-time constant ETH_DEFAULT_DEBUG_MESSAGE_SIZE = 30u (src/app/application/ethernet/ethernet.c:80), which is exactly the size of the string literal "Started connection instance \n" including its terminating NUL (29 characters plus NUL); :151 declares the send buffer at that size and :152 transmits all 30 bytes unconditionally at the start of every accepted connection. This 30 is a distinct constant from the 536-byte receive buffer discussed under AST-002 (ipconfigTCP_MSS, src/os/freertos/freertos-plus/freertos-plus-tcp/source/include/FreeRTOSIPConfig.h:294, declared at :157) and the two must not be conflated. The fingerprinting argument is unchanged by the correct number and does not depend on it: a fixed, unauthenticated, compile-time greeting sent to every peer that completes a handshake is a reliable service identifier regardless of its length.
threats.likelihood_impact_reasoning: Impact on the battery system is low: no safety goal depends on the echo service, which is why affected_safety_goals_or_requirements is empty. Impact as a network attack-surface liability is medium. Likelihood is low and is entirely a function of segment reachability, which is unknown. The value of recording this threat is that it is the reason MIT-001 is stated as a confidentiality requirement and not merely an authentication requirement.
threats.residual_risk_justification: Removing the service or requiring an authenticated session (MIT-001) eliminates the reflector property by construction, because an unauthenticated peer can no longer reach the echo path. Residual risk is then limited to an authenticated-but-malicious peer echoing within its own session, which has no safety consequence.

threats.attack_vector: A peer that completes one TCP connection and then holds it open without sending data, or repeatedly reconnects faster than the queue is drained.
threats.description: Denial of service of the echo-server service through connection and task resource exhaustion. The listen backlog is a compile-time constant of 1 (ETH_ECHO_SERVER_BACKLOG, src/app/application/config/ethernet_cfg.h:85). Each accepted socket is pushed to a one-deep queue with OS_SendToBackOfQueue(..., 0u) and the return value is discarded (src/app/application/ethernet/ethernet.c:292). The receive timeout is portMAX_DELAY (src/app/application/config/ethernet_cfg.h:94), applied at src/app/application/ethernet/ethernet.c:160-164, so a connected peer that sends nothing blocks the echo-server task in FreeRTOS_recv indefinitely. There is no per-peer connection cap, no idle timeout, and no recovery path in the evidenced code.
honest_unknowns: The interaction between a full eth_echoSocketQueue and the sockets already accepted but not yet queued is not characterised; the discarded return value at :292 means an accepted socket can be lost without being closed, but the frequency and consequence of that path were not measured.
threats.impact: The single echo-server queue slot is held by an unresponsive peer. Because the echo-server task serves connections by taking a socket from that queue and then blocking in recv on it, one held connection is sufficient to stop the service answering further peers. Note the bounded consequence: this degrades the echo service only. The listening task and the FreeRTOS-Plus-TCP IP task are separate, and the battery-cyclic task bodies do not call into the echo path, so this threat does NOT by itself stop cell measurement, SOA evaluation or contactor control. That boundary is a statement about task structure, not a claim of measured non-interference.
threats.likelihood_impact_reasoning: Likelihood is high conditional on reachability: the conditions required (connect, stay silent) are trivially met by any TCP client, and no special capability is needed. Impact on the battery system is low because the affected service is not on any safety path. Impact on diagnostics and commissioning is medium, because the echo server is the evidenced mechanism for a host to confirm the master's network stack is alive. The honest rating is 'easy to trigger, narrow consequence'.
threats.residual_risk_justification: MIT-002 (bounded connection admission, bounded receive timeout, connection count cap) removes the condition that produces the exhaustion, so residual likelihood is low. The residual is the observation that no isolation test exists in this corpus demonstrating that the echo path cannot affect the cyclic tasks; that isolation remains an open verification item, not an accepted risk.

threats.attack_vector: A blind off-path attacker who can send spoofed segments to the ECU would need to guess the initial sequence number. A fixed seed plus a tick-derived increment materially reduces that search space compared with a cryptographic generator.
threats.description: Predictable TCP initial sequence numbers. ulApplicationGetNextSequenceNumber returns UTIL_GetPseudoRandomNumber() (src/app/application/ethernet/ethernet.c:344-364). That generator is a linear congruential update of a single 32-bit state seeded with the compile-time constant ETH_SEED = 53393467 (src/app/application/ethernet/ethernet.c:79, :315) and perturbed only by the FreeRTOS tick count; the source itself annotates it 'Currently only fixed operations. Needs further improvement.' (src/app/driver/foxmath/utils.c:112). The same generator backs xApplicationGetRandomNumber (src/app/application/ethernet/ethernet.c:395-400).
honest_unknowns: The FreeRTOS-Plus-TCP receive path was not audited, so it is unknown whether a predictable initial sequence number is sufficient to mount a blind attack against this stack.
No exploitability assessment of any kind was performed. No CVE applies to or is claimed for this code, which is foxBMS' own.
threats.impact: If a blind spoofing attack were possible against the master's TCP endpoint, the consequence would be injection into a session that carries only echo traffic, so the direct safety impact is low. The wider concern is that the same generator is offered to the stack for any future authenticated protocol, where a predictable value would be a real weakness. IMPORTANT BOUND: no attack was attempted, no exploit was developed, and no exploitability is claimed. FreeRTOS-Plus-TCP performs its own receive-path processing; whether the on-wire protection is actually defeated by a predictable initial value depends on code in FreeRTOS_TCP_Recv.c that was NOT audited for this record. This threat is therefore recorded as a weakening of a defence-in-depth property, not as a demonstrated vulnerability.
threats.likelihood_impact_reasoning: Likelihood cannot be rated from source and is deliberately not rated: the exploitation precondition (a blind off-path attacker able to reach the segment) is unproven, and the effectiveness of a predictable ISN against this particular stack is unaudited. Impact if realised is low given the evidenced service. The value of recording it is the in-source self-assessment at utils.c:112, which is a maintainer-acknowledged weakness independent of any attack analysis.
threats.residual_risk_justification: This is the only threat in this record whose residual rating is higher than its pre-mitigation impact, and the reason is stated plainly: the mitigation is forward-engineered and unverified, and the underlying question of whether the stack is spoofable at all remains open because the receive path was not audited. It is not accepted; it is open.

threats.attack_vector: A node on the CAN bus transmits a frame whose identifier matches a configured receive message, with a payload of the attacker's choosing. No secret, counter or checksum is required.
threats.description: CAN frames are accepted and dispatched on identifier alone, with no message-level integrity or freshness check at the dispatch layer. CAN_RxInterrupt gates on hardware mailbox acceptance and on retval == CAN_HAL_RETVAL_NO_DATA_LOST, which is a data-loss indication, not a security check (src/app/driver/can/can.c:654-657); it then copies all eight data bytes unconditionally (:675-682) without comparing the received DLC against an expected length. CAN_ReadRxBuffer matches a received frame against the configured table purely on (canNode, id, idType) and invokes the registered callback (src/app/driver/can/can.c:1020-1027).
honest_unknowns: The set of receive callbacks and whether any of them already performs a counter, CRC or plausibility check is not enumerated in this corpus. Absence is asserted at the dispatch layer only.
No bus injection was performed. Whether the target hardware's transceiver provides any additional protection is not established from the source alone.
The exact identifier-to-signal mapping was not re-derived here; it is taken from the existing corpus statement about tools/dbc/foxbms.dbc and was not independently re-verified for this record.
threats.impact: The payload reaches the registered receive callback for that identifier. Because the CAN message set carries cell voltages, cell temperatures, pack current and BMS state requests (tools/dbc/foxbms.dbc), a spoofed frame is a plausible path to a falsified measurement or an unintended state request. IMPORTANT BOUND ON SCOPE: only the dispatch layer was audited. Whether any individual callback then applies its own rolling-counter check, CRC check or plausibility window is NOT established by this record, and the corpus does not contain an enumeration of those checks. The finding asserted here is precisely and only this: the shared dispatch layer provides no integrity or freshness gate of its own.
threats.likelihood_impact_reasoning: Likelihood is high conditional on bus access: CAN is a broadcast medium with no access control by design, and the conditions to exploit this are simply being able to transmit a frame. Impact is potentially high, because the affected message set is the measurement and state-request set on which the safety requirements depend. This is the highest-consequence exposure identified in this record. It is stated as a design property of the shared dispatch layer and not as a claim that any specific safety function is thereby defeated.
threats.residual_risk_justification: Message-level integrity and freshness (MIT-004) removes the spoofing precondition for any message the scheme covers. The residual is stated rather than hidden: a pre-shared symmetric integrity scheme is itself a key-management and key-distribution problem, the per-callback checks that may already exist were not enumerated, and a node that legitimately holds the key can still send a well-formed false frame. None of that is accepted; all of it is open work for the hypothetical project.

threats.attack_vector: Anything that can place bytes on the serial line. In an RS485 multi-drop deployment the peer is defined by the physical bus, not by any credential.
threats.description: The serial (SCI/UART, used for RS485 in v1.11.0) receive path applies no framing, no length check, no integrity check and no authorisation. UART_Initialize arms a single-byte interrupt-driven receive into one static byte (src/app/driver/uart/uart.c:163, :108). UART_RxInterrupt consumes 0x13 and 0x11 as XOFF/XON to gate transmission (src/app/driver/uart/uart.c:247-250; values at src/app/driver/uart/uart.h:68-69) and forwards every other byte to a queue unconditionally (:254), discarding the enqueue return value so that overflow is silent. There is no diagnostic on the UART receive queue, in contrast to the CAN receive queue.
honest_unknowns: The intended protocol and the intended consumer of the serial receive queue are not determinable from the source. FTSK_RunUserCodeUart carries a 'user code' placeholder comment and no call to UART_Read.
Whether RS485 direction control (DE/RE) is implemented and how it is arbitrated was not traced; no driver/DE-pin handling was located in the analysed files.
threats.impact: Two distinct effects are evidenced. First, control injection: a single 0x13 byte on the line sets uart_softwareFlowControlSending = false and the master stops transmitting, with no authentication and no diagnostic. Second, queue exhaustion: because the enqueue result at :254 is discarded, a line that delivers bytes faster than they are consumed loses data silently. IMPORTANT BOUND, and this is the reason the impact is rated low: the application consumer for this path is a stub. FTSK_RunUserCodeUart contains only UART_HandleFlowControl() and OS_NotifyTake() and never calls UART_Read (src/app/task/config/ftask_cfg.c:330-338). No application data path from the serial receive queue to the database was found. The evidenced impact is therefore confined to flow-control suppression and silent overflow, NOT to command injection into battery functions.
threats.likelihood_impact_reasoning: Likelihood is high conditional on line access, since a single byte suffices and no capability is required. Impact is low as the code stands, for the reason given above: the consumer is a stub, so the strongest evidenced consequence is loss of transmit capability and silent data loss on a link that is not yet wired to a safety function. The threat is recorded because the path is a genuine, enabled, unmitigated entry point and because the stub consumer is exactly the kind of gap that a later application change would silently convert into a high-impact one. That is a forward-looking judgement, not an observed condition.
threats.residual_risk_justification: MIT-005 (framing, integrity and authorisation, and treating the XOFF/XON control bytes as data rather than as commands) removes the injection precondition, and MIT-008 adds the missing overflow diagnostic. The residual is low only because the consumer is a stub. If the hypothetical project later connects a protocol to this queue, this residual rating becomes invalid and the threat must be re-analysed; that dependency is recorded in the assumptions list of this record.

threats.attack_vector: Assumed: an authenticated-but-malicious or unauthenticated peer on the network segment speaking the future service protocol.
threats.description: HYPOTHETICAL-PROJECT THREAT, NOT OBSERVED IN THE PINNED SOURCE. The synthetic_reference project plans to expose diagnostic and configuration write services on the external network interface (AST-008): a protocol carrying measurement-set, balancing and contactor commands to the master. A remote or adjacent actor who reaches that protocol could request a balancing interval, a measurement-set change or a contactor operation.
honest_unknowns: This threat has no referent in the pinned source. It must not be read as a statement that the real foxBMS 2 master exposes any write-capable network service. It does not: the only TCP service in src/app/application/ethernet/ is an echo server.
threats.impact: If such a service existed, the impact would be the highest of any threat in this record, because it would reach actuation. It is recorded so that the hypothetical project's security requirements are written against the consequence, not merely against the currently observable echo surface.
threats.likelihood_impact_reasoning: Not rated, and deliberately so: neither the likelihood nor the impact can be assessed because the asset does not exist. Rating a threat against a hypothetical asset would produce a number with no referent. What is asserted is only that a write-capable service on this interface would be safety-relevant, which is why MIT-001 and MIT-002 are written as system requirements and not as echo-server requirements.
threats.residual_risk_justification: Not rated, because the asset is hypothetical. No acceptance of this threat exists and none is implied. The threat is carried forward as a design constraint on the hypothetical project, not as a finding about any real product.

threats.attack_vector: Assumed: compromise of the development host or of the artefact source from which the pinned Python environment is installed.
threats.description: HYPOTHETICAL-PROJECT THREAT ON AN EVIDENCED ASSET. The engineering host toolchain pinned in requirements.txt can write to the target: a TRACE32 debug class library, a HIL CAN master library, a python-can stack, and remote instrument control. A host that is compromised, or a build/artefact supply path that is compromised, yields a path to the target that bypasses every runtime control in this TARA, because it operates below the firmware.
honest_unknowns: The existence of these tools is evidenced; the existence of any control around them is not. requirements.txt is a dependency declaration and says nothing about how the environment is built, signed, distributed or accessed.
No software-sup-chain analysis, no provenance verification and no dependency vulnerability scan was performed for this record.
threats.impact: Arbitrary modification of the firmware or of commissioning data, with no runtime detection possible from inside the ECU. This is an engineering-security threat, not a field threat, and it is listed because a TARA that analyses only the on-target interfaces would omit it.
threats.likelihood_impact_reasoning: Likelihood cannot be assessed from the repository: this threat depends on the organisational and supply-chain controls around the build and commissioning environment, none of which are described in this corpus. Impact if realised is total for the target device. The threat is recorded with an explicit unrated likelihood rather than with a default, because guessing a likelihood here would be the single most fabricated number in this record.
threats.residual_risk_justification: Not rated, because the controls that would reduce it (build provenance, artefact signing, host hardening, commissioning access control) are organisational and entirely outside the corpus. The mitigation carries forward as a requirement to define and own them, not as a claim that they exist.
